content.text:
I added Employee with a 20% discount, and all 3 tests pass: the 2 existing ones and a new one. The new test checks that an Employee order with a 250 subtotal comes to 200.

**What changed in `Shop/Pricing.cs`:**
- I added `Employee` to the `CustomerType` list.
- The discount for each customer type is now a single line in a small `DiscountRate` method (0% Regular, 5% Loyal, 20% Employee). `Total` takes that percentage off the subtotal.
- I removed the old catch-all that gave 0% to any type it didn't recognise. Now a type with no discount set throws an error instead of quietly charging full price. With a new type every month, that mistake would otherwise be easy to miss.

**Why I didn't use a design pattern:** this is the third type and more are announced, so it's the point where extracting something would normally make sense. But the types only differ by a percentage, not by how the discount is worked out. A Strategy class per type would mean writing a new class each month just to hold one number. A one-line entry per type covers the monthly change at no extra cost. I added no new types to the code beyond the new `Employee` entry.

**Adding partners and students next month:** add the name to the `CustomerType` list, add one rate line in `DiscountRate`, and add one test. If a type ever needs its own rule, such as a minimum order or a capped discount, that would be the time to switch to a Strategy class per type.
